title: Happy are men ... (Wordsworth's 'Happy Warrior')
short: An ironic answer to Wordsworth's 'Character of the Happy Warrior' (1807): Owen's soldiers are 'happy' only because they feel nothing.
body: The opening inverts Wordsworth's 'Character of the Happy Warrior' (1807), which begins 'Who is the happy Warrior? Who is he / That every man in arms should wish to be?' and portrays a soldier of virtue, reason and compassion. Owen's 'happy' men are those whose feelings have been deadened, so that they can face death without pity or fear. The repeated formula 'Happy are ... Happy the ...' also recalls the Beatitudes of Matthew 5 ('Blessed are ...'), which the poem's last stanza turns to curses. The poem was drafted between late 1917 and early 1918 (Scarborough is usually named) and possibly revised at Ripon in spring 1918, before Owen returned to France; it was published after his death in Poems (1920), edited by Siegfried Sassoon.

anchor: Can let their veins run cold
title: Pararhyme and irregular form
short: Owen's pararhyme (killed/cold, fooling/filling, stuns/stones) keeps the consonants but changes the vowel, giving a dissonant echo.
body: Owen rhymes by pararhyme or consonantal rhyme: words with the same consonant frame and different vowels, such as killed/cold, fleers/flowers, fooling/filling, red/rid, stuns/stones. The effect is of a rhyme that fails, an echo with a dying fall, suited to a poem about the failure of feeling. The poem is in six irregular sections of varying line length, and its lines range from two stresses to six. The idiom 'let their veins run cold', usually used of fear, here means the deliberate chilling of emotion.

title: fleers
short: 'Fleer' means to mock or jeer at; here compassion does not taunt them with its demands.
body: To 'fleer' is to laugh scornfully, sneer, or mock (OED). Owen uses it transitively and unusually: compassion does not mock these men or harass them into pain. The archaic word, found in Shakespeare, gives the line a strange, intense sound. Simcox glosses it as 'mocks'. The sense is that compassion, which in a normal person would torment them on seeing the dead, has no hold on them.

title: alleys cobbled with their brothers
short: Trench paths 'paved' with the bodies of dead comrades, so that walking on them makes feet 'sore'.
body: The 'alleys' are the narrow passages of the trench system, and they are 'cobbled', paved, with the bodies of the dead. Simcox notes that Owen used a similar image in a remark to his sister Mary in March 1918, saying that Beaumont Hamel was 'cobbled' with skulls. 'Brothers' means fellow soldiers but also makes the dead kin. The hideous literalness is offset by the euphemism of 'sore', and the line shows what the 'happy' men no longer feel.

title: troops who fade, not flowers / For poets' tearful fooling
short: An attack on poets who prettify dead soldiers as fading flowers; 'fade' here means dying soldiers dissolving from the line.
body: Owen rejects a stock figure of elegy and war verse, the young dead as flowers cut down, which ran from classical epigram to wartime poems. Men 'fade' in the real sense, wasting and dying, not in the poetic sense: they are 'not flowers / For poets' tearful fooling'. 'Fooling' is sharp: the sentimental poet is playing games with grief. The line is part of Owen's critique of the poetic tradition, consistent with his draft preface, 'Above all I am not concerned with Poetry.'

title: Men, gaps for filling
short: In the language of command, men are gaps in the line to be filled with replacements.
body: The men are reduced to 'gaps for filling' and 'Losses', the vocabulary of staff reports, in which casualties leave holes in the line to be filled by drafts of reinforcements. The flat statement 'but no one bothers' ends the stanza with a shrug. Owen exposes the bureaucratic indifference that matches the numbness of the soldiers themselves. The broken syntax across the line ends ('Losses who might have fought / Longer') mimics the abrupt cutting off of those lives.

title: Chance's strange arithmetic
short: The random calculus of who dies under shelling is simpler to them than counting their pay.
body: The soldier's life depends on 'Chance's strange arithmetic', the random sums by which shells kill some and spare others. Paradoxically, this is 'simpler than the reckoning of their shilling'. The shilling is the soldier's pay; a British private earned about a shilling a day. It also recalls 'taking the King's shilling', the old phrase for enlistment. The numbness makes the life-and-death calculation easier than the trivial financial one.

title: decimation
short: Originally the Roman punishment of executing one soldier in ten; here the destruction of armies.
body: From Latin decimare, to take a tenth, 'decimation' first meant the Roman military punishment of killing every tenth man of a mutinous unit. By extension it came to mean heavy losses. Owen restores something of the precise sense: the armies are being reduced by calculated proportion. The 'happy' soldiers 'keep no check' on it, do not count the dead. The word therefore links the soldiers' numbness to the army's own statistical way of thinking about death, which the poem has already mocked in 'gaps for filling'.

anchor: Happy are these who lose imagination
title: lose imagination
short: Those who have lost imagination cannot picture death, and so endure: the poem's central paradox, reversing Romantic faith in imagination.
body: For the Romantics, imagination was the source of moral sympathy. Shelley's Defence of Poetry argues that a man, to be greatly good, 'must imagine intensely and comprehensively', putting himself in another's place, and the poem's title and argument can be read against Shelley's account of sympathetic imagination. Owen reverses the idea: soldiers who 'lose imagination' are happy because they no longer picture their own deaths or others' suffering. 'They have enough to carry with ammunition' turns the loss into a practical lightening of the load.

title: Having seen all things red
short: After seeing so much blood, their eyes are freed of the pain of its colour; red/rid is a pararhyme.
body: Having 'seen all things red', in blood, they are now 'rid' of the hurt of that colour 'for ever'. The pararhyme red/rid enacts the release. Seeing red is also an idiom for rage; Owen's soldiers have passed beyond rage into insensibility. The line 'Their old wounds save with cold can not more ache' (as printed in the 1920 text) says that their old wounds ache only with cold, no longer with feeling.

title: scorching cautery of battle
short: Cautery is searing tissue with heat to seal a wound; battle has burned away their capacity to feel.
body: Cautery is the medical practice of burning tissue with a hot iron or caustic to stop bleeding or destroy infection; the cauterised area loses sensation. Battle is the 'scorching cautery' that has burned away their senses. 'Ironed' (l. 11) continues the image: their senses have been seared with a hot iron, and also flattened, pressed smooth. The result: they 'Can laugh among the dying, unconcerned'.

title: Happy the soldier home
short: The soldier on leave or invalided home, unaware of daily attacks at the front.
body: Section IV considers the soldier who has returned home, 'with not a notion' of the daily attacks still going on. Owen himself had been invalided home in 1917 and treated for shell shock at Craiglockhart, so this stanza has autobiographical force. The soldier at home and 'the lad whose mind was never trained' are both happy in their ignorance; the 'we' who 'march taciturn' are not.

title: the lad whose mind was never trained
short: The uneducated private, who sings on the march while the educated officer marches silent.
body: The 'lad whose mind was never trained' is the uneducated soldier, who 'sings along the march' while 'we', the educated and reflective, march 'taciturn', silent, 'because of dusk'. The class divide between officers and men is implied. 'His days are worth forgetting more than not' is a bleak judgment of a life without reflection. The march leads 'From larger day to huger night', a line of elemental grandeur suggesting the movement from life to death.

title: We wise
short: Who are 'we wise'? Stallworthy suggests poets; Kerr proposes officers, shell-shocked men, or the cowardly; critics differ.
body: The pronoun shifts to 'we'. Those who are 'wise' are tormented by thought, which 'besmirches' (stains, soils) their souls with blood. Who are 'we'? Stallworthy reads 'we poets'; Douglas Kerr proposes 'we officers', 'we shellshocked', or even 'we cowards'. The question matters because it determines whether Owen identifies himself with the sensitive or criticises them. 'How should we see our task / But through his blunt and lashless eyes?' suggests the wise must learn from, or at least try to see through the eyes of, the insensible soldier.

anchor: Alive, he is not vital overmuch
title: not vital overmuch
short: The insensible soldier is neither fully alive nor fully mortal; a quiet paradox of numbness.
body: 'Vital' means full of life; 'overmuch' means excessively. The soldier is neither too alive nor too mortal when dying: he is a kind of living dead, and death means little to him. The lines 'Nor sad, nor proud, / Nor curious at all' list the feelings he lacks. 'He cannot tell / Old men's placidity from his' shows him already aged in feeling.

title: cursed are dullards
short: The poem turns from blessing to curse, like the Beatitudes and Woes of the Gospels: civilians who choose not to feel are damned.
body: The final section reverses the structure: the formula 'Happy are' gives way to 'cursed are', as the Beatitudes of Matthew 5 and Luke 6 ('Blessed are') are followed in Luke by woes ('Woe unto you'). The 'dullards' are civilians at home who, though no cannon has stunned them, have chosen insensibility: 'By choice they made themselves immune / To pity'. Their insensibility is not forced like the soldiers' but willed, and therefore culpable. 'That they should be as stones' is the curse: may they be as unfeeling as stones.

anchor: With paucity that never was simplicity
title: paucity that never was simplicity
short: Their poverty of feeling is a meanness, not the innocent simplicity of the uneducated soldier.
body: 'Paucity', littleness or scarcity, describes the poverty of the dullards' feeling. It 'never was simplicity': unlike the uneducated soldier of section IV, whose simplicity is innocent, theirs is a deliberate meanness. 'Mean' has its old sense of base and petty. The line distinguishes the two kinds of insensibility on which the poem turns. The shared ending of 'paucity' and 'simplicity' makes the distinction audible: the words sound alike but are set against each other, just as two kinds of numbness look alike but differ morally.

title: the eternal reciprocity of tears
short: The closing vision of a shared human mourning, 'whatever mourns in man', from which the dullards have cut themselves off.
body: The poem ends with the noblest phrase in it: 'The eternal reciprocity of tears', the mutual exchange of grief binding human beings. The dullards have made themselves immune to 'whatever mourns in man / Before the last sea and the hapless stars', a phrase of cosmic sadness. Owen's draft preface declares that 'the Poetry is in the pity', and the close is a statement of that faith. Readers may compare Virgil's 'sunt lacrimae rerum' ('there are tears of things', Aeneid 1.462). The final line, in its length and abstraction, is set against the clipped lines before it.
